# Tooltip

A short, non-interactive text hint that names or describes the control it is attached to, shown on hover and keyboard focus.

**Not implemented yet.** This page is the *approved intent* — the props API signed off at gate 1 of the build order, before any React exists. Do not import it; there is nothing to import.

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `tooltip` |
| Family | overlays |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | future / future / future |
| Depends on | — |

## Behavior

A trigger and a short text in the top layer, positioned with CSS anchor positioning — the same machinery as Menu, with no measurement code and no dependency. It is never focusable and never contains anything interactive. Proposed primitive: `getTooltipProps` in `packages/primitives/src/tooltip.ts`, owning the open delay, the hover bridge and Escape; it is a proposal, not yet a commitment.

- **A tooltip only ever repeats or supplements; it never holds the only copy of anything** — It cannot be relied on to appear. There is no hover on a touchscreen, a reader zoomed to 400% may never see it, and a keyboard user only gets it when they happen to focus that exact control. So nothing a reader needs to complete a task can live only in a tooltip. If the content is essential, it is visible text. If it is supplementary and needs to be reachable on touch, it is a Popover the reader opens on purpose.
- **Non-interactive content only, and that is the line between Tooltip and Popover** — A tooltip disappears when the pointer leaves and is never in the tab order, so a link or a button inside it is something a keyboard user can see and can never reach. `content` is typed as a string rather than a node, so the type refuses it instead of the contract asking nicely. Anything with a control in it is a Popover.
- **`relationship` says whether the tooltip is the control's name or a description of it** — The two are wired differently and getting it wrong is audible. For an icon-only button the tooltip text IS the name, so it is wired with `aria-labelledby`. The button still carries an `aria-label` with the same words — Button's contract requires one on every `iconOnly` button, and it is the name that survives wherever the tooltip is not mounted — and because `aria-labelledby` takes precedence over `aria-label`, the name is read once, not twice. For a labelled control the tooltip adds detail, so it is wired with `aria-describedby` and announced after the name. A tooltip that repeats an `aria-label` as a description is read twice; one that names a control that already has a name is ignored. The caller knows which it is, so it is a prop rather than a guess.
- **It meets WCAG 1.4.13: dismissible, hoverable, persistent** — Escape closes it without moving focus, so a reader who summoned it by accident can get rid of it without losing their place. The pointer can travel from the trigger onto the tooltip without it closing, so a magnified reader can move over it to read it. It stays until the pointer leaves both, focus leaves the trigger, or Escape is pressed — never on a timer.
- **Touch: it does not appear, by design** — There is no hover on touch, and the two common substitutes are both worse. Showing on tap would hijack the tap that was meant to activate the control. Showing on long-press collides with the platform's own long-press — text selection, context menus, and on mobile web the browser's link preview. So on a touch pointer the tooltip stays hidden; the accessible name or description is still wired, so VoiceOver and TalkBack users still hear it, and the rule above — nothing essential in a tooltip — is what makes hiding it safe. A pen hover, where the platform reports one, does show it.
- **It works on an `aria-disabled` control, which is one more reason this system does not use `disabled`** — A natively disabled button receives no pointer or focus events, so the most useful tooltip there is — "why can't I press this?" — cannot be shown on it. Because disabled controls here stay focusable and hoverable, the tooltip appears on them like any other control, and `relationship="description"` is how the reason gets announced.
- **An inverse surface, not Menu's** — Approved at gate 1 (decision C3, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). A tooltip is the one overlay that never holds a control and is never opened on purpose, and an inverse chip says so at a glance: it cannot be mistaken for a Menu or a Popover opened from the neighbouring control, both of which are surfaces the reader acts in. The cost is a new pairing — an inverse background and a foreground verified against it in both schemes and in every brand — which is why it goes through the design-tokens skill rather than into this recipe as a palette value.
- **Token gap: the inverse surface and its foreground — needs the design-tokens skill** — The token set has no inverse surface and no foreground verified against one, and inventing either for a single component would be a pairing nobody else can rely on. The pair goes to the design-tokens interview (Purpose / Use when / Don't use for / Pairs with), with its contrast promise added to the token contracts so `npm run themes:check` re-measures it per brand. Until it exists the recipe uses `theme.bg.surface`, `theme.fg.primary` and `theme.border.default` — already verified together — as stand-ins, and gate 2 does not approve the colour lines until the pair is real.
- **Token gap: `motion.delay.hint` — needs the design-tokens skill** — A tooltip must wait before opening, or sweeping the pointer across a toolbar strobes a row of hints. The motion family has durations for transitions and none for a wait, so the recipe borrows `motion.duration.slow-min` (525ms), which happens to be about the right length and is documented for something else entirely. A `motion.delay.*` group, starting with the hint delay, is the proper home. Once one tooltip has opened, moving to a neighbouring trigger opens the next one immediately; that skip is behaviour, not a token.
- **Token gap: `size.measure.*` — needs the design-tokens skill** — A tooltip needs a maximum line length so a long hint wraps instead of spanning the screen. This system has no measure token — the playground already notes it — so the recipe follows Dialog's precedent of multiplying `size.control.lg`, which describes control height and is only a stand-in. Toast and EmptyState hit the same gap; one `size.measure.*` scale would serve all three.
- **Web and native** — Web: the trigger is the caller's element, cloned to receive `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby`; the tooltip is a `role="tooltip"` element carrying the `popover` attribute (`hint` where supported, `manual` otherwise) so it renders in the top layer without a portal. React Native has no hover and no tooltip core component, so nothing is drawn: with `relationship="label"` the text becomes the trigger's `accessibilityLabel`, and with `relationship="description"` it becomes its `accessibilityHint` — which is what both platform screen readers read after the name. `placement` is web-only. The native behaviour is the touch behaviour above, followed through: the information still reaches assistive tech, and nothing is drawn that a finger cannot dismiss. Neither OS control nor Rata-drawn (decision N5): nothing is drawn on native, and the platform screen reader is what delivers the text. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `content` | `string` | — | The hint text. Plain text only. |
| `children` | `ReactElement` | — | The one focusable element the tooltip is attached to. |
| `relationship?` | `"label" \| "description"` | `"description"` | Whether the tooltip names the trigger or describes it. |
| `placement?` | `"block-start" \| "block-end" \| "inline-start" \| "inline-end"` | `"block-start"` | Which side of the trigger the tooltip prefers. |

### `content`

```ts
content: string
```

The hint text. Plain text only.

**Use when**

- A few words: the name of an icon-only control, or one sentence of detail about a labelled one.

**Don't use for**

- Anything the reader needs to finish the task. It will not appear on touch — make it visible text instead.
- A link, a button or formatting. Interactive content belongs in a Popover; the type is a string so it cannot be passed.

**Accessibility** Becomes the trigger's accessible name or description, per `relationship`.

### `children`

```ts
children: ReactElement
```

The one focusable element the tooltip is attached to.

**Use when**

- A `Button`, usually an icon-only one, or a link.

**Don't use for**

- Plain text, an icon or a `div`. A tooltip on something unfocusable cannot be reached by keyboard at all — if the text needs explaining, explain it in visible text.
- A trigger that already opens a Menu or Popover on hover. Two overlays from one control compete.

**Accessibility** Cloned to receive the ARIA reference and the hover, focus and Escape handlers. It must be focusable, or the tooltip is pointer-only.

### `relationship`

```ts
relationship?: "label" | "description" = "description"
```

Whether the tooltip names the trigger or describes it.

**Use when**

- `label` on an icon-only button, with the button's own `aria-label` set to the same words. Button requires it, and `aria-labelledby` wins over it, so the name is read once.
- `description` on a control that already has a name, to add detail — including why an `aria-disabled` control is unavailable.

**Don't use for**

- `description` with the same text as the control's `aria-label`. It is read twice.

**Accessibility** `label` wires `aria-labelledby`; `description` wires `aria-describedby`. On React Native these become `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityHint`.

### `placement`

```ts
placement?: "block-start" | "block-end" | "inline-start" | "inline-end" = "block-start"
```

Which side of the trigger the tooltip prefers.

**Use when**

- `block-end` for a trigger at the top of the viewport, where the default would always flip anyway.

**Don't use for**

- Using it to keep the tooltip on screen. Anchor positioning already flips it near an edge; this states a preference, not a guarantee.

**Accessibility** Visual only. Logical, so `inline-start` is the left in a left-to-right document and the right in a right-to-left one. Web only.

## Use cases

### Naming an icon-only button

A toolbar of icon-only controls, where the tooltip text is the only name each one has.

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Copy token path" relationship="label">
  <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="Copy token path">
    <Icon icon={Copy} />
  </Button>
</Tooltip>
```

`relationship="label"` makes the tooltip the button's name. The `aria-label` stays, with the same words, because Button requires it on every `iconOnly` button; `aria-labelledby` takes precedence, so it is announced once. On touch the tooltip never draws, but the name is still wired, so a screen-reader user hears "Copy token path, button" either way.

### Explaining why a control is unavailable

A button that is `aria-disabled` until something else is done.

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Add a payment method to publish">
  <Button disabled>Publish</Button>
</Tooltip>
```

This works only because disabled Buttons in this system are `aria-disabled` and stay focusable and hoverable — a native `disabled` button gets no events, so its tooltip could never show. The reason must also be somewhere visible on the page, because a touch user will never see this.

### Reaching for the wrong component

A help icon beside a field, whose hint includes a "Learn more" link.

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Used for invoices. Learn more">
  <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="About billing email">
    <Icon icon={CircleHelp} />
  </Button>
</Tooltip>
```

Don't. The link cannot live in a tooltip — it would be visible and unreachable — and the hint would never appear on touch. That is a Popover, opened on purpose by a tap or a press, with a real link inside. Better still, put a short version as the field's own description, where everyone reads it.

## Token recipe

### base

A small transient chip on an inverse surface, so it reads as a passing hint rather than as a menu or a popover. The inverse surface and its foreground do not exist yet, so the colour lines below are the closest existing tokens and are stand-ins; the measurements, shadow and motion are final.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| background | `theme.bg.surface — a stand-in until the inverse surface pair exists; see the token gap decision` |
| color | `theme.fg.primary — a stand-in until the inverse surface pair exists; see the token gap decision` |
| border | `border.default solid theme.border.default — a stand-in until the inverse surface pair exists; see the token gap decision; an inverse chip needs no outline` |
| box-shadow | `theme.elevation.overlay` |
| border-radius | `radius.element` |
| padding-block | `space.1` |
| padding-inline | `space.2` |
| font-size | `type.supporting.size` |
| line-height | `type.supporting.line-height` |
| max-inline-size | `size.control.lg multiplied by 8 — a stand-in, see the token gap decision` |
| gap from the trigger | `space.gap.xs` |
| enter transition | `motion.overlay.duration with motion.easing.enter` |
| exit transition | `motion.overlay.duration with motion.easing.exit` |
| open delay | `motion.duration.slow-min — a stand-in, see the token gap decision` |
